text.en: Nachiketa was a young boy whose father gave away his belongings in a ritual. Nachiketa asked, to whom will you give me? Angry, his father said, to Death. The boy went to Yama, the god of death, and asked him the deepest question: what happens after death? This story from the Katha Upanishad shows how Indian thought loved big questions. In this chapter we meet the roots of India's culture.

The Vedas are the oldest texts of India. They consist of thousands of hymns, prayers in the form of poems and songs, that were recited orally and not written down. They are addressed to many deities such as Indra, Agni, Varuna, Mitra, Sarasvati and Ushas. The last mantras of the Rig Veda call for unity among people. The Vedas are a foundation for many branches of knowledge: art, literature, science, medicine, religion, the art of governance, martial arts and more. Understanding these roots helps us understand India, that is Bharat.
The Upanishads are texts that came later and discuss deep questions about the world, human life and what is eternal. Spirituality is the search for a deeper or higher dimension of life. According to the school of thought called Vedanta, everything, human life, nature and the universe, is one divine essence called brahman, sometimes just tat, that. In a story, Shvetaketu returned after 12 years of study proud of his learning. His father taught him through a salt dissolved in water that the essence is everywhere but unseen, and said, you are That, Shvetaketu. In the Katha Upanishad Nachiketa asked Yama about the soul, which is neither born nor dies. Gargi questioned Yajnavalkya about brahman, the essence that makes the world, the seasons and rivers possible.
Prince Siddhartha was shocked at the age of 29 when he first saw an old man, a sick man and a dead body. He left his home and after years of seeking he realised the truth and became the Buddha, the awakened one. He taught compassion and ahimsa, usually translated as non-violence but originally meaning non-hurting. Monks and nuns formed a sangha and some built monasteries in far-off places. The Jataka tales that have delighted generations of children tell of the Buddha's earlier births and give Buddhist values in simple stories.
Mahavira, whose birthplace was near the city of Vaishali in modern Bihar, taught Jainism, whose teachings include ahimsa, anekantavada (many-sidedness of truth) and aparigraha (non-possession). Jain tales such as the story of Rohineya show how a person guided by Mahavira's words was able to avoid a trap. In both Buddhism and Jainism ahimsa means much more than avoiding harm to a person or animal. It includes thoughts and speech.
The text avoids the word religion and prefers schools of thought and belief systems, because Indian traditions are many and varied. One school did not become popular and disappeared with time. Tribal and folk traditions also count as India's cultural roots. Some tribes have their own versions of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and many tribal groups have the idea of a higher divinity. This variety, with shared values like respect for nature, for knowledge and for non-violence, is a strength of Indian culture.

problem.en: Explain ahimsa with an everyday example.

text.en: Ahimsa means non-hurting, not only not hitting.
For example, not teasing a classmate hurts nobody in body or heart.
So ahimsa includes kind thoughts, words and actions.

problem.en: Which Upanishad story shows that questioning is valued?

text.en: Nachiketa asks Yama about death.
Yama answers him seriously.
So Indian tradition values questions.

prompt.en: What do the Vedas, Upanishads and the teachings of the Buddha and Mahavira share?

requiredIdeas.en: They seek answers to deep questions.
They have shaped India's culture for thousands of years.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the Vedas were written books from the start.
Confusing brahman with the god Brahma.

points.en: The Vedas are the oldest texts, recited orally.
The Upanishads ask deep questions; Vedanta says all is one brahman.
Buddhism and Jainism teach ahimsa and compassion.
Tribal and folk beliefs are also part of India's cultural roots.
